title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Introduction
content: More than 30% of individuals aged 65 and older experience at least one fall each year, and this rate increases to approximately 50% among those aged 85 and older. Of these, 12% to 42% sustain a musculoskeletal injury, resulting in impaired mobility, reduced ability to perform activities of daily living, dehydration, pneumonia, prolonged hospitalization, and a general decline in physical and mental health. [1] Many of these falls, however, are preventable through the use of appropriate screening tools and targeted intervention strategies.

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Introduction
content: Falls are typically multifactorial, arising not only from environmental hazards such as cluttered living spaces or medication-related changes in sensorium, but also from physiological factors including sensorimotor dysfunction, vestibular and spatiotemporal dysregulation, dysautonomia, orthostatic vasculopathy, and biomechanical abnormalities. Several validated screening tools help identify these underlying pathologies, including the Functional Reach Test, the 5-Times Sit-to-Stand Test, the Berg Balance Scale, the Single-Leg Stance Test, and the Tinetti Gait and Balance Test. [2] [3] The latter, also known as the Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA), is widely used across outpatient, inpatient, and rehabilitation settings. [4] While these assessments have been applied in older adults with conditions such as Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, and stroke, their predictive accuracy for identifying individuals at risk of falling remains inconsistent. [5]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Introduction
content: Although clinical balance tests are not a substitute for a comprehensive fall risk assessment, they provide valuable information about balance impairment in older adults. [6] Gait speed and the Timed Up and Go test are beneficial in predicting falls among individuals with dementia who are institutionalized. [7] In contemporary practice, particularly in the post–COVID–19 era, the Tinetti Balance Test has become one of the most effective tools for assessing postural instability and functional decline, making it a crucial component of modern fall risk evaluation. [8]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Procedures
content: The Tinetti Gait and Balance Test is divided into 2 components: gait and balance. The examination should take approximately 10 to 15 minutes to perform, and the examiner should always be near the patient to provide support if the patient exhibits a risk of falling. First, the examiner begins with the balance assessment. The patient starts seated in a hard, armless, stable chair. The patient is asked to rise from the seated position without using their arms or hands. Next, while the patient is standing, the examiner asks the patient to move their feet as close together as possible. The examiner presses the patient’s sternum with the palm 3 times. This can be performed once with the patient’s eyes open, then again with the eyes closed. Last, the patient is asked to turn 360° and sit back in the chair. The scoring system for this portion is divided into 10 standardized subsets, for a total score of 16.

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Procedures
content: The second part of the evaluation assesses gait. The examiner must walk alongside the patient at all times to provide support and guidance. The patient can use an assistive device if preferred. The patient starts by standing, then walks 15 feet at a regular pace, turns, and walks back to the starting point at a quick but safe pace. The scoring system for this portion is divided into 7 standardized subsets, for a total score of 12. The scores from both portions of the examination are combined to obtain a total score. The scoring system is ordinal, ranging from 0 to 2. A score of 0 indicates severe impairment, whereas a score of 2 indicates independence. A lower total score implies greater impairment. [9]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Indications
content: This test should be performed on patients aged 65 and older and those with sarcopenia, frailty syndrome, dementia, hearing or vision impairments, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, stroke, urinary incontinence, diabetes, cardiovascular pathologies, peripheral vascular disorders, anxiety, sleep disorders, and people receiving hemodialysis. Furthermore, this test should be performed on any patient with a history of falls. [11] [12]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Potential Diagnosis
content: All scoring sections and the 3 total scores from this assessment (balance, gait, and total scores) should be considered when creating a differential diagnosis for the patient. The utility of this assessment lies not only in evaluating a patient's fall risk but also in identifying underlying pathologies by interpreting each category and its corresponding subcategories. [9] [13] [14] Interpretation of the balance, gait, and total Tinetti Gait and Balance Test scores offers insight into the physiologic systems underlying mobility deficits.

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Potential Diagnosis
content: Low balance scores may point toward vestibular dysfunction, proprioceptive loss, or visual impairment, while low gait scores often suggest neuromuscular weakness, spasticity, or impaired motor coordination. Clinicians may use these findings to help differentiate age-related changes from pathologic processes such as sarcopenia or frailty syndrome, where diminished muscle strength and endurance lead to shorter step length and reduced stability. Asymmetrical step patterns or bradykinetic movements can indicate extrapyramidal disorders such as Parkinson disease; irregular pacing, truncal ataxia, or foot drop patterns may raise suspicion for multiple sclerosis, stroke, or traumatic brain injury.

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Potential Diagnosis
content: Cognitive and systemic conditions also manifest through the Tinetti Gait and Balance Test. Dementia and sleep disorders often result in inconsistent pacing, inattentive turns, and decreased postural adaptation. Anxiety may produce guarded, hesitant gait initiation, whereas urinary incontinence can be associated with hurried or unstable gait linked to frontal lobe dysfunction. Peripheral causes such as diabetic neuropathy or peripheral vascular disease may present as reduced step height, uneven weight-bearing, or compensatory trunk sway.

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Potential Diagnosis
content: Additionally, patients with cardiovascular pathologies or those receiving hemodialysis may demonstrate fatigue-related gait instability, orthostatic imbalance, or slowed recovery from perturbation. By integrating these findings within an interprofessional team, including primary care, neurology, physical therapy, nursing, and occupational therapy, clinicians can correlate gait and balance subtest results with medical history and diagnostic imaging to uncover underlying disease mechanisms. This transforms the Tinetti Gait and Balance Test from a fall-risk checklist into a dynamic diagnostic tool that guides individualized, system-specific interventions, thereby improving patient outcomes.

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Normal and Critical Findings
content: A patient scoring 18 or below is considered at high risk for falls, while a score between 19 and 23 indicates a moderate risk (see Table 2 ). Scores of 24 or higher indicate a low risk of falling.

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Interfering Factors
content: The outcome of this assessment is primarily affected by patient comorbidities and exercise tolerance. [9] The Tinetti Gait and Balance Test involves standing, turning, and walking, so it cannot be performed safely in patients who are unstable. Individuals with acute illness, significant cardiovascular compromise, orthostatic hypotension, severe musculoskeletal limitations, or marked exercise intolerance are at increased risk of falls or other adverse events during testing. In these patients, attempting the assessment could produce unreliable or misleading results, as their performance may reflect temporary instability or medical limitations rather than true balance or gait ability. [9]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Complications
content: Complications associated with the Tinetti Gait and Balance Test are generally uncommon, making it a safe and practical tool for assessing fall risk in older adults. [2] The examiner acts as a spotter during testing to mitigate the risk of falls, particularly in patients with impaired balance, frailty, or significant mobility limitations. Despite these precautions, minor complications may occur, including musculoskeletal complaints such as sprains, strains, or transient joint discomfort, especially in patients with underlying arthritis, recent injury, or limited range of motion. Rarely, patients with cardiovascular instability, severe orthostatic hypotension, or acute illness may experience lightheadedness, dizziness, or fatigue during the test. Proper pre-assessment screening, careful monitoring, and immediate intervention if symptoms arise are essential to ensure patient safety and maintain the reliability of the assessment. [2] [9]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Clinical Significance
content: For the Tinetti Gait and Balance Test, the interrater reliability, sensitivity, and specificity for predicting falls vary in the literature. This is primarily due to the patient populations selected in the various studies and slight variations in the assessment performed. Faber et al suggest that the interrater reliability for the balance assessment and total score was good, with an R score of 0.4 to 0.93. However, the interrater reliability for the gait assessment was lower, with R scores ranging from 0.72 to 0.89. The sensitivity and specificity in predicting falls were 62.5% to 66.1% for the total score. The results of another study reported sensitivities ranging from 64% to 95.5% and specificities from 60% to 100%. [16]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Clinical Significance
content: Although the assessment may not capture all fall-risk patients, it is cheap, simple, reproducible, and may shed light on underlying pathologies affecting gait or balance. [17] This test is a screening tool used to identify a patient's risk of falling. If the patient has a high total score but a low score in 1 of the scoring categories, that aspect must be addressed, as it can be a risk factor for a future fall. Furthermore, if the patient has a low total score, the clinician should identify any underlying pathology and implement appropriate management strategies. Moreover, the clinician should ensure that these patients have access to appropriate support and a safe home environment to reduce their fall risk. [18] [19]

title: Tinetti Gait and Balance Test -- Clinical Significance
content: While the Tinetti Gait and Balance Test may not identify all patients at risk for falls, it remains a low-cost, simple, and reproducible tool that can highlight underlying pathologies affecting gait or balance. [17] Clinicians should address low scores in individual categories even when the total score is high, as these deficits can contribute to future fall risk. In patients with low total scores, it is crucial to identify underlying pathologies, implement appropriate management strategies, and ensure that patients have adequate support and a safe home environment to reduce their fall risk. [18] [19]
